title: A resource ceiling stops the request that broke it: the allocator publishes into the word compiled code polls, the value allocators refuse in front of the allocation, and a store no request owns is accounted apart
scope:
how `rule:errors/on-limit`'s memory and CPU ceilings are enforced against a request that
reaches no member call and no back edge that looks at them, and whose bytes a request is measured
against. It changes nothing about what a breach *reports* — the tier it lands in, the
`LimitReport` it carries, whether it is catchable — and it does not give a freed block per-request
provenance, which waits on the request arena.

summary.headline: A resource ceiling stops the request that broke it, where the resource goes
summary.body:
A request that exceeds its memory or CPU budget is stopped by the runtime, not by a check the
program happens to run. The allocator raises a flag the compiled code polls on every loop, which
bounds a runaway loop; each value allocation asks before it allocates, which bounds a single
huge operation a loop check would reach too late; and a watchdog samples each core's CPU clock.
Bytes held by a store that outlives requests, such as a process-wide cache, are accounted to the
process, so no request is charged or credited for them.
